Naked Truth: De ce nu mai participăm la (toate) licitațiile? 🤷‍♀️

Din experiența noastră, am învățat că nu orice oportunitate merită automat toate resursele, timpul și energia pe care suntem tentați să le investim.

Licitațiile pot implica săptămâni sau luni de muncă, strategie și mobilizarea mai multor oameni. Iar uneori, raportul dintre efort și rezultat ridică întrebări importante.

1. Investiția de resurse nu vine întotdeauna cu transparență și feedback.

Poți petrece luni pregătind documentații, adaptând soluții și construind o ofertă competitivă, pentru ca procesul să se oprească fără feedback. Nu afli ce nu a funcționat, unde ai pierdut puncte sau ce a făcut diferența.

Înțelegem că feedbackul detaliat nu este întotdeauna posibil, dar în parteneriatele B2B transparența și comunicarea ar trebui să fie parte dintr-o relație profesională sănătoasă.

2. Unde se termină evaluarea competențelor și unde începe exploatarea ideilor?

O licitație presupune adesea mai mult decât o ofertă financiară. Înseamnă strategie, brainstorming, soluții personalizate și idei dezvoltate special pentru nevoile clientului.

Practic, pui pe masă o parte din expertiza și know-how-ul echipei tale. Problema apare când acestea sunt analizate și valorificate, fără ca furnizorul care le-a dezvoltat să ajungă să le implementeze.

Nu orice idee devine automat proprietatea celui care o formulează, dar timpul și munca intelectuală a participanților merită tratate cu responsabilitate profesională.

True story 

În urmă cu 3 ani, am câștigat o licitație pentru recrutarea a minimum 50 de poziții IT & Engineering. Procesul de licitație a durat peste 6 luni, iar negocierea contractului încă 4. În total, 10 luni de efort și resurse investite, o miză importantă, mai ales pentru un start-up.

Deși contractul avea o durată de 3 ani, am încercat în repetate rânduri să inițiem o discuție cu departamentul HR, să înțelegem hiring plan-ul, prioritățile și cum puteam deveni un sprijin real.

Răspunsurile primite au fost dezinteresate, uneori chiar agresive, iar insistența de a solicita o întâlnire a fost interpretată drept lipsă de respect.

Deznodământul? În 3 ani, FlexibleHR nu a primit nici măcar o poziție în lucru. O singură întâlnire cu HR, obținută cu greu, ne-a clarificat că nu exista o intenție reală de colaborare.

Efort și implicare 100%. Rezultat: ZERO.

Sigur, contractul nu obliga clientul la un anumit volum de recrutări și nu presupunea exclusivitate. Dar dincolo de documentele semnate, un parteneriat presupune intenție reală, comunicare și deschidere reciprocă.

LESSON LEARNED: Un contract câștigat nu garantează un parteneriat.

Nu orice contract merită câștigat cu orice preț și nu orice oportunitate este, în realitate, o oportunitate de business.

Te-ai regăsit într-o astfel de situație? Cum ai reacționat? Feedbackul comunității noastre ne ajută să învățăm și să facem mai bine. 🙏

Karnataka will teach artificial intelligence to Class 9 students in eighteen hundred government high schools this academic year.

Python. Computer vision. Natural language processing. Topics many of us first met in college are now going into a Class 9 timetable.

I think this is the right direction. A child in a government school deserves the same early start as a child in an expensive private school. AI will be part of almost every job these students apply for.

But one line in the news stayed with me. The department has started hiring guest teachers to deliver the course.

Guest teachers are often the most stretched people in a school. Short contracts, long commutes, very little time for their own training. Now we are asking them to teach a subject that changes every few months.

A curriculum is only as strong as the teacher standing in front of the class. Not the syllabus. The support.

If this is going to work, teachers need three things before students do. Real training, with time set aside for it. A small circle of other AI teachers they can call when a lesson goes wrong. And tools that take routine checking off their desk, so their hours go into explaining, not marking.

Karnataka has taken the first step. The second step is the teacher.

Teachers and school leaders, if your school started teaching AI next term, what support would your teachers need first?

If you're hiring a creative strategist right now, you're not competing with other brands. You're competing with the freelance market.
⠀
Last year I got around 50 offers. Most were full-time, one brand, $4-6K a month on average. It doesn't make sense if you can work with a few brands and make over $15K.
⠀
Here's the paradox I keep seeing in job descriptions.
⠀
Brands want a strategist who owns everything. Runs the research and analysis. Briefs and manages the team. Controls the process. Knows AI generation and automation tools. Jumps into an overloaded brand workflow and gets it moving fast. Doesn't need direction at every step.
⠀
But think about what's going on in the head of someone who can actually do all that. If they don't need managing, they can run this for three or four brands at once. With their own workflow and no extra layers of approvals, they spend less time on ops and more on what moves performance.
⠀
That person is rarely looking to be tied to one brand.
⠀
Partly it's just insurance. Lose one contract and the other two still pay the bills. Tie yourself to one brand, and if something goes wrong there, often nothing to do with creative strategy, you lose everything overnight.
⠀
The market is starting to adjust. I'm seeing more offers built as a $4-8K base plus a percentage tied to results. Some brands now agree to part-time, retainer or contract work. Still a minority. Most still want full-time.
⠀
And there's a bonus most brands miss. A strategist working across several brands brings in what's working in other niches: hooks, formats, angles. A strategist inside one brand only ever sees one account.
⠀
I've done this many times. You spot an early winner in one niche, an angle nobody in the other niches has used yet, bring it to another brand you work with, and it becomes a winner there too.
⠀
If you need someone fully independent, hire them the way independent people want to work. Tie it to performance, that's fair. Just don't make full-time the only option.
⠀
And I'm 200% sure of this: if you turn out to be a good fit for each other, that person will happily consider a full-time role on terms that work for both sides.
⠀
Founders, CMOs and HR: how are you structuring creative strategy hires right now?
⠀
Creative strategists: are you full-time, or on contract and retainer?
⠀

Accuracy is the wrong first question for an AI hiring tool. Vendors love to open with accuracy. 94 percent this, 97 percent that. It sounds great in a demo.

I would ask something else first: when the tool gets it wrong, who finds out? A wrong answer on a spreadsheet is a typo. A wrong answer on a resume screen is a person who never hears back and never knows why.

A tool that is right most of the time and has no human check is a bigger risk than a tool that is right a little less often and has a clear path to review. Regulators are starting to say the same thing, and ADMT is one example.

So before you sign the contract, ask to see the appeal process. If the vendor cannot show you one, you already have your answer.

Job quality is easy to talk about and hard to measure. The European Commission's annual employment report puts some evidence behind it.

In its 2026 European Employment and Social Outlook, published on 13 October, the Commission says the quality of jobs in the EU has improved over the past decade, with progress on pay, job security and working time.

The report also shows where the gaps are:
Better job quality is more common in information and communication, finance and insurance, public administration, and professional, scientific and technical activities.
Poorer job quality is more common in accommodation and food services, administrative and support services, and some lower skilled service jobs.
Shortage occupations often come with less secure contracts and more atypical working hours.
Some countries worsened on two or more indicators even though the EU trend was positive.

Two points on context. Minimum wages have risen since the EU Minimum Wages Directive, especially in lower wage countries. And the Commission expects an energy shock to slow hiring in 2026: about 440,000 fewer jobs created than expected, which its own coverage describes as slower hiring, not a wave of redundancies.

For early career workers, the report notes that entry level and routine jobs face particular pressure from AI, while also potentially seeing the biggest immediate productivity gains from AI tools. How that plays out depends on how AI is introduced and governed.

A caution: these are sector averages built from indicators on pay, security and working time. They cannot tell you how a particular employer treats its people, so the posting, the contract and the interview still matter. The Commission plans to present a Quality Jobs Act later this year.

When you compare offers, we help with the practical part: 1.1M+ vacancies across 16 European countries and a free salary calculator at newluxjob.com, and you can upload your resume to let AI match you to roles. Listings are not rated for job quality.

Back in February, I picked up a requirement from a client I was working closely with at the time.

I had a really strong contractor go through the interview process, but on this occasion, they were pipped to the post by another excellent candidate who had slightly more specific experience for that particular role.

Fast forward a few months, the business has been through a restructure, there’s a new hiring manager and a very similar requirement comes around.

After speaking with a few candidates and not quite finding the right fit, I remembered the contractor I’d spoken with back in February.

Although they weren’t quite right for the original position, their skill set was actually a much closer match for what the new team needed.

Luckily, we’d stayed in touch and they were still interested.

A couple of interviews later and they’ve secured a 12-month contract. They’re now absolutely smashing it.

It’s a good reminder of how important it is to maintain relationships with contractors, even when there’s no immediate opportunity on the table.

I’d like to think I’m pretty good at staying in touch with the contractors I’ve built relationships with, but nobody’s perfect and it’s certainly something I want to double down on and improve going into 2027.

With that in mind, I’m making December a bit of a reset.

Whether we’ve spoken about opportunities this year or haven’t been in touch for a while, I’d love to reconnect.

I’d like to get a better understanding of what everyone’s looking for heading into 2027, including availability, contract end dates, rate expectations and the type of projects you’d be interested in.

That way, when the right opportunity comes around, we’re already one step ahead.

Always worth staying in touch. Sometimes the right opportunity just comes along at the right time.

I hear this from founders and hiring heads, and it is a fair question.

A contract developer builds something for you. Then the contract ends. If nobody planned the handover, the knowledge leaves with them.

The fix is simple, and it starts before the last week.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲𝘀:
• Clean, readable code with short comments where the logic is not obvious
• A simple document: what was built, how it runs and how to fix common problems
• A walkthrough session with the person who will own it next
• Access list: what the developer could reach, and when it is removed
• A short list of what is not done yet, so nothing is a surprise

𝗔 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗵𝗮𝗯𝗶𝘁𝘀:
• Agree on the handover in the first week, not the last
• Ask for small updates through the project, not one big report at the end
• Keep a named owner on your side for every part of the work

When the handover is done well, you have options. You can extend the contract, hire the developer full-time through contract-to-hire, or let your own team take over with confidence.

The contract ends. The work stays with you.

Checking filename.endswith(".pdf") in production is like hiring a bank security guard who checks IDs by asking people what their name is.

In Enterprise Content Management (ECM), incoming files are messy. Scanners dump extensionless blobs, users rename plain text files to .bin, and Legal suddenly needs support for a brand-new format next Tuesday. If your ingestion endpoint relies on a giant if/elif chain over filename extensions, you are building a maintenance trap—and if you parse massive PDFs synchronously inside an async def FastAPI route, you are freezing your entire server for every other user.

In Part 4 of my 10-part hands-on series—where we build OpenText-style enterprise systems in Python from scratch using strict Test-Driven Development—we solve multi-format capture by building IngestPipe.

Think of IngestPipe as an Automated Mailroom Assembly Line:

True Binary MIME Sniffing: We inspect the first 2 KB of raw magic bytes using python-magic (libmagic), completely ignoring spoofed or missing file extensions and rejecting unsupported binaries with a clean 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Plugin Architecture (IngestHandler): Every format worker (TextHandler, PDFHandler, ImageHandler) implements one normalized IngestedDocument contract and registers onto the conveyor belt without touching core orchestration code.

Non-Blocking Concurrency: CPU-bound pypdf parsing and UTF-8 decoding are offloaded via asyncio.to_thread() so the FastAPI event loop stays responsive under load.

Strategy-Injected AI Vision OCR: Scanned images (PNG, JPEG, TIFF) delegate extraction to an injected OCRClient strategy—verified deterministically in milliseconds with Pytest and rendered inside a live Streamlit + Monaco Editor (streamlit-ace) workbench.

'Is AI the slow poison killing an entire generation?'

If AI does the work junior employees learn by doing, where will you get your next experts and managers from? We're walking collectively into a problem here aren't we?

Vincent Barat of Albert raised this question of the impact on AI on junior hiring and the future workforce at the SWP Conference in London. He didn't hold back. 

Think back to a mistake you learned from early in your career. Think about how you learned what good looks like, what the right quality output needs to be, and so on. I have learned through my career that learning requires tension - something harder than the easy path, that forces the development of new neural pathways. A Socratic approach to AI prompt creation may help by teaching us how to think to get to the answers we need, but it is still a substitute. 

The key risks will not be around AI adoption and digital augmentation, it will be whether in the future we will be able to discern data quality and impact, whether we collaborate well with others, what has already been learned from history and what is genuinely new and value-add and how to navigate organisational politics with developed levels of EQ.

Pick one role that’s changing. Ask someone who does it which tasks taught them to spot a mistake. Where will the next recruit get that experience?

Last week a learning lead told me they’d spent most of this year’s budget on contractors for their AI projects. Next year, same plan.

Then I saw Randstad’s new numbers: only 3% of employers say upskilling their own people is their main way of closing AI skill gaps. Most are hiring or bringing in contractors.

I get why. It’s faster. But the skills everyone wants, things like AI governance, are exactly the ones the market can’t supply quickly enough. So you end up paying more every year for the same skills, and they leave when the contract does.

What I’ve seen work is simpler than people expect. Pick the roles that matter most, train people on the tools you actually use, and get them certified so the skill counts for something in their career. Use contractors to cover the gap while that happens, not forever.

Curious whether others are seeing the same thing. Is your team mostly hiring for AI skills right now, or building them?

I've read AI policies that run to 30 pages. Nobody follows them, because nobody has read them.

A policy people actually follow fits on one page and answers five questions:

1. Which tools can I use? Named, not "approved tools".
2. What can I put into them? Green, amber, red data, with examples from our own work.
3. What must I check before using the result? Facts, numbers, sources, names.
4. Where is AI not allowed? For example: final decisions about hiring, credit, health or anything with legal effect, without a person reviewing it.
5. Who do I ask, and how do I suggest a new tool?

That's it. The details, contracts and risk assessments can live in an appendix for the people who need them.

Two things that make the difference in practice:

Write it with a few people who actually use AI daily, not only legal and IT.
Review it every six months. The tools change faster than any policy.

A one-page policy that's 80% right beats a perfect one that sits in a folder.

Does your company have an AI policy, and could an employee tell you what's in it?

Private equity cannot rely on cheap debt and rising market prices anymore.
With higher interest rates, returns come from one thing only: making portfolio companies run better.

Many operators thought AI would be an easy shortcut. The data says otherwise:
• 95 percent of corporate AI projects fail to produce real profit (MIT).
• Only 6 percent of private equity firms see major gains in daily operations today (McKinsey).
• 40 percent of buyers discount acquisition offers by 5 percent or more for messy tech (BCG).

If you are an operating partner , here is the six step playbook to turn software into actual cash earnings:

Test claims strictly before buying
Apply a pass or fail test during diligence. If a company cannot prove daily production, clear ownership, verified math, full cloud running costs, and safe data access, remove those promised savings from your purchase price.

Count real cash only
Real profit equals actual money saved minus new computer bills. Only count payroll savings when real jobs or outside contracts end. Never count avoided future hiring as Day 1 profit.

Fix core systems in the first 100 days
Do not put smart automation on top of broken software. Spend the first 100 days cleaning customer records, upgrading core accounting databases, and killing shared passwords.

Start in the finance department
Enforce a six month payback rule. If a project cannot prove cash gains in two quarters, kill it. Finance is the best entry point because accounting numbers are clean, audited, and show direct dollar savings fast.

Use four checkpoints to stop failing tests
Most companies fail because they never cancel bad projects. Enforce four gates: Admit, Validate, Build, and Copy. If a pilot fails to prove its value quickly, shut it down.

Track running costs and secure logins
Model fees and cloud computing add up fast. Track bills down to the specific task so software costs do not eat your margins. Give every automated tool its own secure account and an emergency off switch.


Stop treating AI like an open ended experiment. 
Fix your basic data, track every dollar of running costs, kill failing pilots early, and turn technology into verified operating profit.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴: "𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗲?" 🤔

I hear this from founders and hiring heads, and it is a fair question.

A contract developer builds something for you. Then the contract ends. If nobody planned the handover, the knowledge leaves with them.

The fix is simple, and it starts before the last week.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲𝘀:
• Clean, readable code with short comments where the logic is not obvious
• A simple document: what was built, how it runs and how to fix common problems
• A walkthrough session with the person who will own it next
• Access list: what the developer could reach, and when it is removed
• A short list of what is not done yet, so nothing is a surprise

𝗔 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗵𝗮𝗯𝗶𝘁𝘀:
• Agree on the handover in the first week, not the last
• Ask for small updates through the project, not one big report at the end
• Keep a named owner on your side for every part of the work

When the handover is done well, you have options. You can extend the contract, hire the developer full-time through contract-to-hire, or let your own team take over with confidence.

The contract ends. The work stays with you.
